title: Vercel Tracing is now generally available
excerpt: Vercel Tracing is now generally available on all plans. You can now search and inspect traces from the dashboard or the Vercel CLI , and new Next.js projects get tracing by default. Pricing is unchanged from the beta. Browse and search traces in the dashboard In beta, you could only open a trace per request from the Logs page. The new Traces page shows every trace and span in one place, for a project or your whole team. Switch between a Spans list and a Traces list, filter each, and search with Kibana Query Language (KQL). A Live mode streams new traces as they arrive. A query like span.name:db* AND span.duration > 500 narrows to slow database spans by name and duration. Search traces from the CLI The Traces page uses the same KQL as vercel traces search --query , so a query built in the dashboard runs in the CLI unchanged. Search covers every project in your team, or one project with the --project flag. Inspect a single trace with vercel traces inspect <request-id> , and manage a project's sampling rules with vercel traces config . Automatic tracing for new Next.js projects In beta, nothing was collected until you added a sampling rule. Starting with Next.js 16.5, new projects created on Vercel that include at least one Node.js function get tracing turned on after their first successful build. Vercel adds one sampling rule tracing 100% of requests in all environments and injects instrumentation at build time, so traces include Next.js framework spans with no setup. To opt out, remove all sampling rules in Settings → Tracing. Longer retention In beta, traces followed your runtime log retention. Hobby now keeps traces for 3 days instead of 1 hour, Pro for 14 days instead of 1 day, and Enterprise for 14 days instead of 3 days. Read the Tracing documentation to learn more. Read more
summary: Vercel's tracing tool, which shows how a web request moves through an app and where it slows down, is now available to everyone. You can search traces in the dashboard or the command line, and new Next.js projects turn it on automatically; traces are also kept longer.

title: Chat SDK agents can now stream generative UI with json-render
excerpt: You can now stream generative UI from your Chat SDK agent with json-render . With a typed catalog of components, the agent writes a JSON spec that json-render converts into a Chat SDK card. Each adapter then posts the card in its platform’s native format, such as Block Kit on Slack and Adaptive Cards on Teams. The catalog covers tables, charts, buttons, and more, so there’s no separate tool to build and maintain for each message shape. Stream cards as the model writes streamCard posts the card once its root element has content and updates the message as new elements stream in. Edits go out at most once every 500 ms by default, which matches Chat SDK’s streaming interval. Once the stream ends, the message shows the final, validated card. Validate specs and enforce platform limits toCard checks every element’s props against its component schema and throws CardSpecError for an invalid spec. Each problem gets its own readable issue, so you can send the list back to the model for a corrected spec. Platforms cap what a single message can hold, and Chat SDK adapters degrade content past those caps. The Slack adapter, for example, turns a second table into a code block. Pass limits to reject those specs instead. Read the documentation to get started, or try the playground . Read more
summary: Chat SDK agents can now stream rich messages like tables, charts, and buttons as they are written, using a shared set of building blocks. The same message is shown in each chat app's own style, and invalid messages can be caught and fixed before they are sent.

title: Ampersand from Humans& now available on AI Gateway
excerpt: Ampersand from Humans& is now available on AI Gateway for free through November 13, 2026. Ampersand is a language model built to take part in group conversations, such as a team chat, and to decide on each turn whether to speak or stay quiet. It is designed to understand individual and shared goals, help people work through disagreements, and recognize when a contribution would be useful. That can mean asking a clarifying question, sharing relevant context, or waiting while people respond to one another. Your application exposes these actions as caller-defined function tools . send_message delivers a contribution, while pass leaves the conversation quiet until the next human message. Your application executes both tools and records their results. Leave tool choice at its default, since Ampersand accepts auto and none but rejects required and named tool choices. Call it through the AI SDK , the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API , or a coding agent. Use humansand/ampersand-v0.1 as the model name: The first human message invites a contribution; the second asks Ampersand to wait. In a chat application, call the handler when a new human message arrives. Handling pass records the waiting action without posting a message or starting another model turn. For a deployed chat application, persist the response, history, and delivery receipts in durable storage. Retry uncertain delivery with the saved action and the same receipt, process messages sequentially per conversation, and check conversation access before posting. To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup: Then select humansand/ampersand-v0.1 in the agent. See the coding agents guide for details. Try Ampersand in the model playground . title: Safe and Efficient Multi-Epoch Embedding Training
excerpt: Authors: Shruthi Hariharan | Machine Learning Engineer II; Konish Dutta | Machine Learning Engineer II; Abhinav Naikawadi | Sr. Machine Learning Engineer; Zhihua Zhang | Machine Learning Engineer II; Rakshita Nagalla | Sr. Machine Learning Engineer; Kousik Rajesh* | Machine Learning Engineer II; Matt Lawhon | Staff Machine Learning Engineer Tags: Machine Learning, Infrastructure, Recommendation Systems Content Track: Technical Discussion / Architecture of big components * == work done while at Pinterest Introduction Large ID embedding tables underpin some of the largest modeling advances at Pinterest, including teacher-model scaling and cross-domain pretraining for ranking and retrieval. These tables are first pre-trained to learn broadly useful Pin representations and then fine-tuned as part of the downstream surface-specific ranking model. Here, we’ll focus on the Homefeed ranking model. The strength of the embedding tables comes from their enormous capacity to absorb information about billions of Pins and learn rich representations. That power, however, is coupled with fragile training dynamics that have historically constrained fine-tuning to one epoch. That compromise has become increasingly dissatisfactory; single-epoch fine-tuning prevents us from effectively optimizing our models over small, fresh datasets in retraining, and disproportionately harms effective representation learning of certain components of our ranking model which benefit from longer training, like Vision Language Models (VLMs). A one-epoch ceiling forces every component of our model to learn on the schedule of its most training-sensitive component. When trained longer, two problems appear: Model quality degrades sharply. In Homefeed ranking, we saw nearly a 6% decline in our offline save metric when extending training from one epoch to two epochs. GPU waste from communication-bound training accumulates. Distributed embedding lookup and synchronization overhead created large idle periods in the training loop, leaving GPUs waiting on communication rather than performing useful computation. Background The “one-epoch” phenomenon of large ID embedding tables is well documented in recommendation systems literature. Their enormous capacity, combined with sparse and long-tailed updates, makes it easy for the model to “memorize” individual IDs associated with repeated examples rather than learn representations that generalize. Prior work at Pinterest had already shown that multi-epoch ID embedding training does not fail in every setting. Taming the One-Epoch Phenomenon in Online Recommendation System by Two-stage Contrastive ID Pre-training demonstrated that embeddings themselves could be pretrained for multiple epochs using a contrastive-only pretraining objective before being transferred to downstream models for finetuning. We were interested in multi-epoch post-training : once the pretrained embeddings are part of the Homefeed ranking model, could we fine-tune them for multiple epochs without catastrophic overfitting? Related work from Pinterest Ads explored strategies to train longer in post-training, including frequency-adaptive updates and larger learning rates; however, the ID embedding tables in this setting did not exhibit the same catastrophic multi-epoch degradation we observed in Homefeed. Making multi-epoch training safe Freezing as a method to identify the problem To answer why we saw a nearly 6% decline in the offline save metric when extending training to two epochs, we isolated each component to determine whether the whole model was overfitting or whether the regression was concentrated in a particular module. The embedding table emerged as the dominant source of the regression: when we froze the table, the multi-epoch regression disappeared and the result beat the single-epoch trained model. Over three epochs, we saw a +1.25% gain over the one-epoch model. Although freezing the embedding table immediately unlocked multi-epoch training, it pre
summary: Pinterest found that its large ID embedding tables in the Homefeed ranking model get worse when trained for two epochs, with an offline save metric dropping nearly 6%. Freezing those tables during extra training removed the drop and gave a small gain over one epoch.

title: Agent Distraction
excerpt: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

title: The post-quantum future of web privacy
excerpt: The highest priorities for the transition to post-quantum cryptography are the basic building blocks of authenticated key-agreement protocols such as TLS. Without these building blocks in place, secure communication on the Internet will not be possible once cryptographically relevant quantum computers come online. However, today we rely on quantum-vulnerable cryptography for much more than TLS. Privacy Pass is a protocol used by site operators like Cloudflare to help protect applications from abuse. One way we do this is by rate limiting individual clients so that no one client consumes too many of the site's resources. Normally this involves some combination of friction or loss of privacy for users: CAPTCHAs or other challenges to moderate traffic, along with accounts and fingerprinting to identify traffic.Privacy Pass was designed to avoid this tradeoff between friction and privacy. The basic idea is that a client gets issued a number of tokens , which they can redeem in exchange for access to the site. Crucially, each token is unlinkable to the client it was issued to, ensuring the client can use the site as they always had without sacrificing privacy. With 10 years of deployment experience under our belts — using Privacy Pass for applications such as privacy proxies (like iCloud Private Relay) and relays (like Privacy Gateway) — we, along with others , are collaborating to bring the next generation of this technology to the web. One of our goals is to develop more sophisticated tools for managing agentic traffic that would otherwise consume too many resources and degrade performance for human visitors. Another goal is to foster a more open ecosystem by making it easier for more types of clients to participate. Achieving these goals requires developing new capabilities beyond what Privacy Pass offers today. Given the trajectory, in this post we look at the prospects for post-quantum. In fact, we're in better shape than one might think. Privacy Pass still relies on classical cryptography, like RSA and elliptic curves. This means that a quantum attacker will be able to forge tokens at will and use them to bypass whatever security mechanism the site operator wants to implement (such as rate limiting). On the other hand, Privacy Pass is unconditionally private, meaning no attacker, quantum or not, can link the redemption of a token to its issuance. What's more, the new capabilities we're developing for this new generation of private authentication technology can and will be instantiated in a way that upholds the same guarantee: your interaction remains private even after Q-day. This gives us a little breathing room, but we will need an alternative soon. This is an active area of research that has made significant strides in recent years. Still, just as is the case with other aspects of the transition, the primary challenge is the sheer size of post-quantum alternatives: ML-DSA-44 signatures are a whopping 2,420 bytes, while ECDSA-P256 signatures are just 64 bytes. And there's not much hope for drop-in replacements any time soon. Just as for TLS, we'll have to settle for primitives with higher cost and re-engineer our systems to bear this cost . But what will those primitives be? In this post, we'll explore one potential future for post-quantum privacy on the web, made possible by a recent breakthrough in the design of blind signatures. What we need to build: a brief look at MOLE Let's start with an overview of this new technology, which is presently called MOLE ("Moderation Of unLinkable Endorsements"). We'll have much more to say about MOLE later on, but for now we'll highlight the details that are most relevant to cryptography. One of the core components of Privacy Pass is a blind signature scheme, which allows a client to obtain a signature under an issuer's secret key without revealing to the issuer the message that it signed. The client can then reveal the message and blind signature later on without linking the signature
summary: Cloudflare describes how Privacy Pass, a tool that lets sites limit heavy users without tracking them, could be made safe against future quantum computers. A new design called MOLE may keep user privacy intact even after such computers exist, though the post notes the new versions are much larger and costlier to run.

title: Inside GitHub’s new Git storage architecture
excerpt: Last week at GitHub Universe, we announced our new Git storage architecture, capable of handling thousands of writes per second with reads that scale on demand. Through internal testing, we’ve demonstrated the ability to support 5,000 concurrent agents working on a repository, sending 7,200 pushes per second to a repo, all while serving read traffic with consistently low latency. This new architecture is the foundation for GitHub to support agentic development for hundreds of millions of developers, and we’ve been building it underneath GitHub while it keeps running. Over the past year, agents changed what a busy repository looks like on GitHub. In our first post in this series, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation Git storage architecture: minimize coordination, and decouple storage from compute. In our last post , we covered the bridge: moving 99.99999% of repositories into Azure, scoping the write quorum to individual references, and standing up virtual replicas backed by Azure Blob Storage. We also left off with an observation: very little of a write needs to be ordered. Git objects are immutable and named by their contents, meaning two writers can store them at the same time without agreeing on anything. The part of a push that needs agreement is the reference update, and a reference update is tiny in comparison. Virtual replicas were the first step toward building around that, and the means by which we onboard repositories to the new architecture. The rest of the architecture builds on that observation. Only reference updates need agreement. That lets the parts of Git infrastructure that used to be tightly coupled (storing data, serving requests, and maintaining repositories) scale independently. For developers, Git stays Git: they push, fetch, and branch the same way, with the same protections in place. Below, we walk through the requirements behind the design, follow a request through the system, and dive deep into two of its components. Building for agent scale We think about the scale of the GitHub platform along two axes: Horizontal scale is how many developers and agents can work across many repositories. Many of GitHub’s current approaches on this axis have been battle-tested over the years and are carried forward to the new architecture: partitioning of tenants across infrastructure, isolation and/or fairness enforcement of tenant traffic, and load-aware routing, to name a few. Vertical scale is how many developers and agents can work on one repository. As agents write more code, we expect individual repositories to get larger and busier, so most of our requirements came from the vertical axis. Today, the busiest repositories on GitHub.com receive at most dozens of writes in a single second, typically in short bursts. As more of that work shifts to agents running in parallel and around the clock, we expect those bursts to become a sustained rate within the next year. Each push leads to more reads: CI runs, deployment systems pull the new commit, and other agents fetch it for context. This read fan-out results in a large amplification effect on overall traffic that scales with writes. We’re already seeing this trend play out on repositories at the top of the curve. The chart below shows daily requests to one repository on GitHub from March to May, when its traffic grew about 4x. Its growth has continued on an exponential trajectory since then. We have to plan for a world where agent-driven development keeps accelerating at this speed. Instead of planning for the next increment, we set a target of at least two orders of magnitude more scale. For a single repository, that meant the new architecture needed to: Accept thousands of writes per second. Support multiple writer nodes. There are two reasons for this: Experience has taught us that indexing incoming packs and checking object connectivity are the most CPU-expensive parts of a write, and that cost scales with the size of the write, so a sin
summary: GitHub announced a new way of storing Git code that can handle thousands of changes per second on one repository. In internal tests it handled 5,000 agents working at once, which matters as AI agents make busy repositories far more common.

title: How two engineer side projects became the agent taking action inside Dropbox
excerpt: AI can help people turn an idea into a first draft, but getting to something usable depends on more than a prompt. It needs the files and context behind the request, software to carry out the work, and a way for people to review and refine the result. With the new Dropbox experience , we’re bringing those pieces together where people already keep their work, so they can ask questions about their content and request tasks such as organizing folders, renaming files, and preparing materials to share. Letting an agent change those files meant giving it a controlled place to work, enforcing permissions, and recording its changes so people could review and undo them. The agent behind those tasks started as two experiments, each approaching the same problem from a different angle. Daniel Reiter Horn and Rich Chan, engineers at Dropbox, were using coding agents for tasks beyond writing software, including designing 3D-printed models and filing expense reports. Both encountered the same challenge: giving an agent access to their Dropbox files while retaining control over what it changed and a way to recover things when something went wrong. Melding those experiments meant connecting the agent to both the files in Dropbox and the safeguards already built around them. Access to the filesystem let the agent work directly with files, while version history provided a record of changes that could support rollback. An isolated workspace gave it somewhere to run installed software, with permission checks outside that workspace controlling what it could access and change. The overall system brought those pieces together for customers , letting them follow the work, approve access, and review the results. Connecting an agent to the work already in Dropbox The early projects of both engineers exposed different parts of the challenge, starting with the software an agent needed in order to get the work done. For Daniel, the need for the right software became clear when he wanted to build a futuristic cityscape model that his son could turn into a diorama. The family laptop had no 3D modeling software, so he put together a sandbox, an isolated computing environment, with a coding agent and specialized software. He connected it to Dropbox using rclone, a tool that let the agent work with his online files as if they were stored inside the sandbox. Through an experimental command-line interface, Daniel could describe changes, preview the model on dropbox.com , and refine the design until it was ready to print overnight. The prototype ran outside the Dropbox web experience and didn’t yet have agent permission controls or conversation-specific undo, but it showed that an agent could produce something useful directly in Dropbox without relying on software installed on someone’s laptop. --> Rich, meanwhile, had been approaching the same problem through the desktop app. Each week, he used a coding agent to turn receipt images into expense reports, but every run meant copying the receipts out of Dropbox to a location the agent could access. He spent a week building a graphical interface directly into the Dropbox desktop app so he could run an agent with access to his Dropbox files. The prototype combined usability, safety, and permission controls, giving Rich confidence to use it on his own data. He could then process his receipts and handle routine tasks directly from the app, without copying files elsewhere. The interface also connected to the Dropbox folder pickers, live previews, and revision history, letting Rich open the files being changed and trace a revision back to its conversation. Those connections made it possible to follow the agent’s work through the files themselves, providing a foundation for reviewing and undoing changes later. The experiments complemented each other. title: How AI-assisted development helped us build the new Dropbox experience
excerpt: For three years, we’ve been working toward a new Dropbox experience that helps people do more with their files, from finding a project decision to getting a folder ready to share. Today, we’re beginning to roll that experience out to customers. But getting here meant changing how we build software. We had complex integrations to tackle and a deadline to meet, and AI-assisted development helped us take on work that would've previously been difficult to complete in time for launch. The new Dropbox experience puts that investment into practice by helping customers understand what’s in their files and get work done with them. Ask Dropbox what changed in a project folder, and it answers with sources you can open and check. Ask it to organize a folder, rename files based on their contents, or combine documents into a PDF, and it shows a plan you can review and edit before approving. Dropbox only reads and acts on content you already have permission to access, and supported file changes can be undone. And the results stay in Dropbox, where teams can review, share, and keep working with them. Delivering that experience meant building new capabilities on web and bringing them into desktop, with shared code that let us develop features for both applications. Engineers took broader ownership of product decisions and brought quality checks into development from the start. As the work progressed, we moved from using AI to help with individual coding steps to delegating defined tasks—including implementation and testing—for engineers to review. Together, those changes helped us deliver a product years in the making within an ambitious launch timeline. Bringing more of Dropbox into desktop We began with a broad product direction and a lot of details to work out. We needed to turn that direction into specific experiences people could use, including a fuller desktop app. Desktop had primarily focused on keeping files in sync, while web already supported richer ways to browse and work with content. We wanted to build on that foundation and bring both existing features and new capabilities developed on web into desktop without rebuilding everything separately for each platform. The difficulty was that web and desktop had grown around different needs. They used different tools to build and release software and handled tasks such as signing in, navigating between pages, and retrieving data differently. A web feature could depend on services that desktop didn’t provide in the same way. Before we could reuse it, engineers needed to identify those dependencies and work out how to support them—a substantial integration effort to complete before our November launch deadline. During our Hackathon in May, engineers built a working prototype that explored two possible approaches to tackling this problem, and AI helped them trace dependencies, identify platform-specific assumptions, and test the integration. One approach displayed the existing All Files page inside a desktop-specific window using Electron, the framework behind desktop’s interface. An embedded web view—a browser surface inside the app—let us bring the existing web browsing experience into desktop quickly. The second approach imported selected web components directly into desktop’s user interface. These individual building blocks required more integration work but gave us greater control over how they fit into the desktop app. The working prototype gave Product and Design something concrete to try before we committed to a larger architectural change. Engineers turned directional designs into usable flows, surfaced missing states, and proposed options as platform constraints became clear. Product and Design worked through those choices as engineers built the features, allowing us to refine the experience as we learned. We found that both approaches had a place: complete web pages where we wanted close parity, and individual components where we needed more control. AI reduced the effort of tes
summary: Dropbox is starting to roll out a new experience that lets people ask questions about their files, organize folders, and combine documents, with changes shown for review first. title: Agents aren’t humans (but they kinda are)
excerpt: AI Agents now act on the web for millions of people. To a Site, an Agent can take many forms. It may be indistinguishable from a human user carrying out a task, or it might look like one visitor carrying many Users. This removes the ability for the Site to recognize, serve, and hold accountable the user or users behind the Agent, and causes the Site to face the costs when something goes wrong. This post argues that in order for Sites to maximize the access they provide to Agents, the ecosystem must develop new mechanisms to preserve the relationship between Sites and Users. Traditionally, in Security and Fraud Prevention, that requires three things: Identity, Reputation, and Accountability, allowing Sites to answer: Is the person acting being truthful about who they are? Is that person trustworthy? And who answers for the action? “Personal AI Agents” (“Agents” for short) are automations that take instructions from a human (“User”) and pursue a goal by controlling a cloud computer or browser. They are usually hosted and maintained by an “Operator” as part of a managed service or consumer offering. Examples include Muse from Meta and dots from OpenAI, and more are launching all the time. Agents can potentially take any action online that their User could, without the limits that hold humans back. They don't tire, they run around the clock, they act in parallel, and they put up with friction no person would. Much of the web, from how Sites plan capacity to how they make money, assumes those limits. Fundamentally, remotely hosted Agents are intermediaries . An intermediary is anything that sits between a User and a Site, so the Site sees it instead of the User. Agents are the newest kind of intermediary, but intermediaries have existed for a long time. Cloud browsers (hosted browsers that software controls on a User's behalf) and Proxies (services that relay a User's traffic, including VPNs) are intermediaries too. What has changed is the trajectory. Agentic traffic is growing rapidly and may eclipse traditional human browsing on the Internet in the near future. This forces a reckoning for anyone operating a Site today. Historically, a Site could simply block intermediary traffic and require Users to disable the intermediary service. That stops working when the majority of traffic is agentic. Once blocking is no longer viable, Site Operators are left with the problem that intermediaries have always created. The Site loses direct information about the User and must decide whether to trust the intermediary without it. This post covers Agents hosted somewhere other than the User's device. Local agents (e.g. OpenClaw) or Agents running in the User's own browser, on their own device, are out of scope of the primary topic addressed by this post (see below, "On open source and local Agents"). This post rests on one principle: The Intermediation Principle : The business relationship between Users and Sites, and each participant’s security responsibilities, must be upheld regardless of intermediation. A Site needs new tools to recognize, serve, and hold accountable a User acting through an Agent just as it could if that User had visited directly. The Agent, and the Operator behind it, must be recognizable and accountable too, because an Agent can do what no User could. Agents are able to scale human access almost without limit, so they create new risks, even for behavior that was previously benign. The intermediary problem Meet Ezra. Ezra works as a personal assistant for people in her city. Her best client is Amy, a local CEO, but she also works for Bob, Charlie, and Debra. She runs their errands: groceries, appointments, paperwork, and flights. Ezra blends into the crowd. The corner grocer used to know Amy. He knew what she bought and set aside what he thought she'd like. Now only Ezra comes in, carrying orders for four people, and the grocer can't tell whose preferences are whose. He doesn't want to turn Ezra away, because she brings hi
summary: AI agents now act on websites for people, but sites can't easily tell who is really behind them or hold anyone responsible. The post argues that new ways to verify identity, build trust, and assign accountability are needed so sites can serve these agents safely.

title: Workflow SDK adds idempotent starts
excerpt: The Workflow SDK 's start() function can now admit a run and claim a hook in one atomic step. Duplicate workflow starts fail safely. The atomic start replaces the previous getHookByToken() -then- start() pattern, whose gap between the lookup and the start left a documented duplicate-start race. Subscribe to messages inside the run The claimed Hook exists from the moment the run is admitted, so resumeHook works even before the run begins executing, and early payloads are buffered and delivered in order. Inside the workflow, createHook({ token }) with the same token binds to the already-claimed hook: guaranteed, registering nothing new, adding no step, and resolving getConflict() to null . Idempotency with no extra code The token is the idempotency key, and it comes from your own domain: an order ID, an invoice ID, an import ID, or a request ID. The token alone guarantees idempotency. Exactly one run owns it, and a duplicate start() throws HookConflictError carrying the owner's conflictingRunId and never becomes a run. The workflow doesn't have to open the hook at all, and if it never does, the token was only an idempotency key and the run completes normally. Setting experimental_minRetention keeps the token unavailable after the run ends, counted from start() , so late duplicates are still refused. Upgrade to workflow 5.3.1 and read the idempotency documentation to get started. Read more
summary: Vercel's Workflow SDK now lets a job start and claim its ID in one safe step, so duplicate starts are refused instead of running twice. This fixes a known race where two near-simultaneous starts could both succeed.

title: Introducing Vercel Schedules
excerpt: Cron jobs are useful for work that needs to happen regularly. You can use them to do things such as back up your database on a schedule, or keep data in sync between two systems. You define them once in code and then can update them by editing their config and redeploying. But today, agents interact with users as work evolves, and schedules need to be updated in real time. We built Vercel Schedules to allow agents and applications to create, change, or cancel one-time and recurring schedules through code, without redeploying. What are Vercel Schedules? Schedules builds on the static approach used by Vercel Cron Jobs , but are designed to let users and agents decide when work should happen while your application is still running. A schedule tells Vercel when to trigger a task and where to send it. Your application provides the code that carries out the work. You can use schedules for both static and dynamic jobs: Static schedules keep the timing in vercel.json or Build Output API configuration and sync when you deploy. You can use them to call private functions or HTTP paths, or send messages to Queue topics . Dynamic schedules let your app create and manage schedules through the JS SDK , CLI , or API as it runs. They support one-time and recurring work through Queue topics. You can also test scheduled work on Preview deployments and in custom environments before running it in Production. How Schedules works Take this example: A user could ask an agent with web access, “Tomorrow morning, summarize the top five stories on Hacker News.” The traditional solution would be storing the request and its schedule time in a database, then using a cron job to check for work that is due. With Schedules, an agent can create a schedule that records the request and when to run it, without a separate database and polling job. The example below defines an AI SDK tool that gives an agent this capability. When the task is due, Vercel uses Queues to deliver the saved request to your app. Your app provides code to read that request , check the user’s current permissions, and start the agent. The agent fetches the top five Hacker News posts with a web tool, then returns a summary for your app to save for the user. If you already build agents with fx’s JavaScript library, libfx or Pi’s agent library , you can add a similar scheduling tool. The eve agent framework uses Vercel Schedules to provide dynamic scheduling tools for production agents hosted on Vercel. Run recurring application jobs You can schedule recurring work with Vercel Schedules. Schedules can be created dynamically via the JS SDK , API , and CLI , or set up in your project’s configuration. For example, to create a job that cleans up expired records every day, you could define a schedule that invokes a private function in your chosen time zone: Vercel calls this cleanup code directly, without exposing it at a public URL. It checks that each call comes from the scheduling service, so you don’t have to add that check yourself. If your app already uses the Nitro 3 server framework, its experimental integration lets you run the recurring jobs in your existing scheduledTasks configuration as private functions. You can also try the agent task and cleanup locally with vercel dev , then test them on a Preview branch or in a custom environment before production. Use Run Schedule in your project’s Schedules tab to try either task without waiting, and see when past runs happened. Get started Vercel Schedules is now in Public Beta , and you can use it for the recurring tasks your application already runs. When a user or agent chooses when work should happen, your code can create and manage a schedule for that task. To get started, check out the Vercel Schedules skill and read the documentation . Read more
summary: Vercel released Schedules, a tool that lets apps and AI agents create, change, or cancel one-time and recurring jobs while the app is running, without redeploying. It is now in public beta.

title: Scaling Model Evaluation at Pinterest with Ray (Part 4)
excerpt: Vishnu Arun | Tech Lead, Feature Importance Platform; Anderson Lam | Sr Software Engineer; Andrew Qiu | Machine Learning Engineer I; Helena Xu | Data Scientist I; Tianyou Wang | Data Scientist II Introduction In our multi-part blog series, we have discussed why we chose Ray as a last mile data processing framework, how we integrated Ray into our existing ML Training Infrastructure, and how we enabled efficient Batch Inference at scale. In this blog post, we will discuss how we were able to apply Ray to another critical part of our ML Infrastructure stack: Model Evaluation . In the Ray Batch Inference Blog Post , we ended on a section on accumulators (counters that would allow us to calculate metrics like ROC-AUC and cross entropy). This post is where those accumulators pay off: a model evaluation platform that combines the strengths of Ray and Apache Spark to compute metrics efficiently at scale. Model evaluation may appear to be a relatively straightforward step after inference or training. But as ML workflows scale, evaluation quickly becomes an infrastructure challenge. Systems that run many experiments in parallel, such as feature importance, must efficiently compute and aggregate metrics over large volumes of inference data, as shown in Diagram 1. Later in this post, we’ll show how we amortize the metrics compute step, overlapping it with inference for minimal added runtime cost, cutting end-to-end evaluation time by up to 32% while scaling linearly as we run more experiments. Diagram 1 : Depicts a feature importance system’s architecture. We illustrate a multi-head model with h heads and metrics calculated per head. In this type of workflow, metrics are calculated for each experiment and model head. Note: We omit a batched view of this data found in large scale production ML systems for simplicity. Terminology Feature Importance (FI): A technique for quantifying how much each input feature contributes to a model’s predictions. In this post, we will reference a perturbation-based method where we perturb one or more columns, run inference, and compare the results against an unperturbed dataset. Experiment / baseline: One perturbed run vs. the unperturbed run. Model head: One output of a multi-task model. Batch: an arbitrary, compute-sized group of rows. This is the unit of data that one Ray task processes. Bucket: a batch that is group-preserving. It contains one or more complete segments, and no segment may span buckets. Segment: The semantic unit over which a group-wise metric is defined, such as a request. Serde [serialization/ deserialization]: The process and cost of writing data out and reading it back. Background Traditionally, evaluation and inference are two separate stacks stitched together. Diagram 2 below contrasts that unfused pipeline against the fused pipeline we’ll build up over the rest of this post. Diagram 2 : Unfused (top) vs. fused (bottom) inference-and-metrics compute. In the unfused lane, inference and metrics run as separate jobs connected by a serialize/persist/deserialize handoff; in the fused lane, metrics are computed per batch inside the Ray inference job via the shared object store. Red denotes the cross-stack handoff removed by fusion. Concretely, this evaluation step is typically implemented as a Apache Spark job that computes metrics across one or more inference experiments. As shown in the diagram above, we previously used Ray inference to write predictions to S3, then have a follow-up compute job to reread all this data and compute the metrics. For a FI run, this approach introduces two sources of overhead: Cluster startup : Acquiring and warming up a cluster for the metric job. Data movement: Writing predictions to S3 and reading them back to compute metrics. Because inference is done in batches, and metrics typically depend on all of the inference results, the unfused approach can be used to calculate any metric. To save the overheads, we need to fuse the stages, but this also implies
summary: Pinterest describes how it now computes model evaluation metrics during the same Ray job that runs model predictions, instead of in a separate Spark job that rereads saved results. They report this cuts end-to-end evaluation time by up to 32% and scales as more experiments run.

title: See the agents, set the terms: new visibility and control for personal agents
excerpt: Personal agents are the intermediary between humans and the Internet, turning a person’s instructions into requests and actions on websites. A customer might ask a personal agent to compare products across your site, find support articles, or complete a purchase. To a site owner, all three interactions show up as automated traffic — and without a clear view of which agents are visiting and what they are doing, it can be difficult to know whether that traffic is helping your business or creating risk. Blocking agents altogether can feel like the safest choice, but it can mean losing customers. Better visibility into agent activity allows you to decide what access makes sense for your site. Today, we’re launching new analytics to help you understand how personal agents access your site on behalf of humans, along with more granular access policies to put those decisions into practice. Together, they let you welcome agents on your own terms, and in ways that support your business. See how agents access your site Knowing which agent is behind a request turns unexplained automated traffic into traffic you can act on with confidence. Cloudflare maintains the largest verified bot directory in the world, and we are now bringing that intelligence into your traffic details. In Security Analytics, the Bot Analysis chart now shows Personal Assistants as a new category, next to Verified Bot, Likely Human, Likely Automated, and Automated. Security teams can select it to see only personal agent traffic over time. In Top statistics, a new Personal Assistants widget lists which agents are visiting your site and how many requests each one sends. Filter on one agent and every other widget updates to show only its traffic details: the paths it requests, the status codes it receives, and the networks it comes from. At a glance, you can see whether an agent is logging in, reading your product pages, reaching your checkout, or hitting errors on pages it cannot use. For sites that protect user accounts with Account Abuse Protection (currently in early access), site owners and fraud teams are able to see which user each agent represents. The population overview page shows which personal agents are active across your users and how many accounts use them, so you can determine whether agent traffic is a meaningful part of your business. Every login and sign-up event now shows whether a personal agent made the request, and which one. Fraud teams can filter accounts by AI assistant events or number of AI assistants. Additionally, each user's account overview shows the agents acting for that account. A fraud analyst investigating an unusual login can tell whether it came from an agent the customer has relied on for weeks, or from an agent that appeared for the first time today and needs a closer look. If it looks like an attacker is using an agent on an account, fraud analysts can mitigate that account directly, with a WAF rule on its Hashed User ID, without blocking the agent for everyone else who relies on it. Together, these views give you a clearer basis for deciding which personal agents to welcome, limit, or block. Set access policies that reflect your preferences We introduced AI bot policies this summer so site owners could make separate access control choices for AI bots used for Search, Training, and Agent behaviors. Now we’re expanding the existing Agents policy to include granular control options for supported personal agents. To reflect this broader scope, we’re renaming the setting AI Crawler and Agent access policies . In Security Settings , you can set an overall Agents policy, then choose a different policy for each supported personal agent: Allow (do not block) , Block on pages with ads , or Block . For example, you can set the overall Agents policy to Block on pages with ads , then choose Allow (do not block) for a supported personal agent you want to welcome. Your existing Search and Training policies stay as they are. You can also make t
summary: Cloudflare launched new tools that show which personal AI agents visit a website and what they do there, plus settings to allow or block each agent. Site owners can use this to decide which agents help their business and which pose risk.

title: Amazon S3 Tables now offer managed migration of Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg
excerpt: Today, we’re announcing a simple, cost-effective path for data lake modernization. Amazon S3 Tables now support managed migration of your Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg . Migration works with Parquet tables in Amazon S3 that are registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog and allows you to upgrade your data lake with no pipelines to build or compute to provision, while production workloads keep running. Apache Iceberg has become the open standard for large analytics datasets. It lets you manage petabyte-scale tables with features like schema evolution, hidden partitioning, and time travel queries, while keeping your data open and queryable with any Iceberg-compatible engine. Amazon S3 Tables offer fully managed storage purpose-built to keep Iceberg tables performant and cost-effective as they grow, with features like automatic maintenance, optimization, replication, and S3 Intelligent-Tiering built-in. What is new Previously, migrating Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg could take weeks of engineering work to build and manage the required infrastructure. Converting data types and building rollback capabilities added operational complexity. Now, this is available as a managed, API-driven operation. S3 Tables handle the entire migration workflow, including data validation, compatibility checks, type conversions, file recompression, and compaction. Before copying any data, S3 Tables identify every source object in scope and generate a compatibility report. You can sync as many times as you need without stopping writes to your source table, except for a few minutes during cutover. Once you are ready, you can complete the migration, minimizing time that tables are offline. Compared to self-managed approaches, S3 Tables managed migrations are cost-effective because you pay only for the data copied, with no charge for the Hive-to-Iceberg conversion, and source objects in S3 Intelligent-Tiering stay in their current access tier. A first look at the migration To migrate an AWS Glue Hive table, choose your destination table bucket in the S3 console , then choose Create table from migration . Create a namespace and table name for your destination Iceberg table. The destination table is created using recommended default settings tuned for query performance and storage efficiency. When you start the migration, S3 Tables validate the source table, generate a compatibility report, and begin copying data. The destination table is read-only during the migration. Once you complete migration, the destination table is promoted to read-write. You can begin working with your data right away using a direct integration with Amazon Athena and Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio in the AWS console, or use any tool compatible with the Apache Iceberg REST API to directly query the tables. To learn more, visit the S3 Tables migration documentation . You can also use AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) , AWS SDKs , or the Agent Toolkit for AWS . For example, set up migration jobs and call the start-table-migration command. cat > /tmp/start-migration.json <<'EOF' { "roleARN": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/S3TablesMigrationRole", "destinationTable": { "tableBucketARN": "arn:aws:s3tables:us-east-1:123456789012:bucket/my-destination-bucket", "namespace": "mynamespace", "name": "my_destination_table", "encryptionConfiguration": { "sseAlgorithm": "aws:kms", "kmsKeyArn": "arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:123456789012:key/1234abcd-12ab-34cd-56ef-1234567890ab" }, "storageClassConfiguration": { "storageClass": "INTELLIGENT_TIERING" }, "tags": { "team": "s3tables", "purpose": "migration" }, "properties": { "writeFormat": "parquet", "icebergFormatVersion": 2, "compressionCodec": "zstd", "dictionaryEncoding": true }, "schema": { "type": "struct", "schemaId": 0, "identifierFieldIds": [1], "fields": [ { "id": 1, "name": "id", "type": "long", "required": true, "doc": "primary key" }, { "id": 2, "name": "payload", "type": "string", "required": false } ] }, "icebergSortOrder": { "o
summary: Amazon S3 Tables now offers a managed way to move old Hive-style data tables to the newer Apache Iceberg format, without building custom pipelines. The tool checks compatibility, copies data, and lets the old table keep running until a short cutover, so teams can modernize their data storage faster and pay only for data copied.

title: Vercel Security Review now in public beta
excerpt: Vercel Security Review is now in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams. Once enabled, every push to a connected GitHub repository is automatically reviewed for vulnerabilities, and findings are reported in the Vulnerabilities dashboard . What triggers a review Security Review runs automatically when code is pushed to a connected GitHub repository. Because reviews start from push events rather than pull requests, direct and force pushes to your production branch are reviewed as well. Every project affected by a single push is reviewed together. What a finding includes Each finding records the project, environment, branch, and commit, with a summary, a suggested fix, and an AI-generated severity rating. Security Review adds its own GitHub check to each commit it reviews. When there's a pull request, it also posts findings as review comments that link back to each finding. On public repositories, finding details stay in the dashboard. Fixes and resolution Clicking Fix with Vercel Agent on a vulnerability report hands the finding to Vercel Agent, which proposes a fix and opens a pull request for you to review. Nothing merges until you approve it. To fix findings with your coding agent instead, use vercel security vulnerabilities in the Vercel CLI, or copy any finding as Markdown or JSON. Security policies Teams can write security policies in plain language, for all projects or specific ones, to give Security Review more context about how they build. Set a team policy in Agent settings and a project policy in the project's Security settings. Limitations Security Review analyzes source code. It isn't a security audit, and it doesn't perform runtime or penetration testing. It helps you find vulnerabilities but doesn't guarantee your application is free of them. Pricing Security Review is billed at the Vercel Agent rate : provider inference at the underlying token rate with no markup, plus the Vercel Token Rate of $0.25 per million tokens (input, cached, output). Reviews run on each push to GitHub, so cost scales with how often you push and how much code changes. Security reviews are free until November 10, 2026, and fixes made with Vercel Agent are billed at the Vercel Agent rate. Enable Security Review in your team’s Agent settings , or read the documentation and the announcement to learn more. The CLI command needs Vercel CLI 65.10.0 or later. Read more
summary: Vercel now offers Security Review in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams. It automatically scans each code push to connected GitHub repositories for security problems, and it is free until November 10, 2026.

title: Diagnose Vercel CLI setup problems with vercel doctor
excerpt: Vercel CLI now includes vercel doctor , which checks your setup and shows the command that fixes each problem it finds. It checks the CLI version and install, your login and current team, the project link, and your project configuration in vercel.json . It also reports active incidents from the Vercel status page. Each check reports OK, Warning, Failed, or Skipped. When vercel upgrade can't update the installed CLI, the install check shows where the CLI runs from and how to reinstall it. Doctor runs without a login or a linked project, and it never prompts, logs in, or links a project, so coding agents can run it before guessing at a fix. Add --json to get each check's status and suggested commands as structured output. Update to the latest CLI version and run vercel doctor to check your setup, or read the doctor command reference. Read more
summary: Vercel's command-line tool now has a "vercel doctor" command that checks your setup and suggests a fix for each problem it finds. It also reports active Vercel outages, and it runs safely without changing anything, so it's useful for both people and coding tools.

title: How OpenEvidence scales medical search for 650K doctors
excerpt: OpenEvidence on Vercel Serves 650,000 doctors with medical search Completes production deployments in about five minutes Absorbs traffic spikes without additional capacity provisioning Reduced serverless spend by 90% with Fluid compute Updates doctor- and patient-facing applications independently OpenEvidence helps physicians find medical evidence during care, whether they’re checking a dosage on intensive care rounds or handling a case outside their specialty without a specialist nearby. Answers draw on peer-reviewed literature and include citations, so doctors can examine the sources behind them. OpenEvidence’s small team began using Vercel to get early experiments online and kept that workflow as the product grew, relying on the platform to handle web deployments and capacity. Building software physicians depend on The stakes are different when software helps inform medical decisions. An incorrect answer can affect how a doctor treats a patient, while an unavailable application can cut off access to evidence when it is needed. OpenEvidence supported more than 20 million clinical consultations in January 2026 . The company also reported that more than 100 million Americans were treated by doctors using OpenEvidence in 2025 . "Honestly, life or death is not inaccurate," says Kush Khosla, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. "We operate in situations where it's an ER and they really need to know what's going on. Uptime is very, very important to us." "A lot of doctors and medical professionals are used to really outdated software," says Andy Yoon, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. A more modern experience still needs to meet physicians' expectations of speed, stability, clarity, and information they can trust. The small team needs a way to test updates to the web application before putting them into production and to roll back if something goes wrong. Keeping releases simple as the audience grows Andy recalls why Vercel suited the team he joined at OpenEvidence. "I was pretty much the only engineer on our team coming from an actual frontend background," he says. "Most of our team works in Python and machine learning." He adds, "Given the makeup of our engineering team, Vercel really scaled with our needs so well." The team builds its physician-facing web application with the Next.js framework . When engineers push changes to a development branch, Vercel builds and deploys a preview , giving them a link they can use for live demos and share with colleagues to try new features. Pushing or merging into the production branch then triggers the production build and deployment. If a release needs reverting, the team can roll back to a previous deployment . That workflow lets the team release multiple times a day, with each change becoming available to a physician audience that Kush thinks about whenever he ships something: More doctors without more provisioning Keeping that application available means handling demand the team can’t always anticipate. Andy was scrolling through Slack when he saw the message that OpenEvidence had gone viral on TikTok, reaching around two million views in under a week. He watched traffic climb and checked the logs. Response times stayed fast and error rates remained near zero , and with no additional capacity to provision, he went back to his work. Beyond sudden spikes, the team has accommodated sustained growth without rebuilding the web application. "Not once have I had to think, now that we have five times as many doctors, what's happening to page loads or time to first paint," Kush says. "The scaling has happened so naturally that we end up focusing on other things." A 90% drop in serverless spend As usage grew, VP of Engineering Micah Smith was watching compute costs. summary: OpenEvidence, a medical search tool used by about 650,000 doctors, runs its web app on Vercel, which lets its small team ship updates several times a day and handle traffic spikes without adding servers. title: How Mercor ships internal apps and billions of production tokens on one platform
excerpt: Mercor on Vercel Batch jobs cut from 12 hours to 2 hours 18M requests and 63B tokens routed through AI Gateway in 10 days Expert access provisioned in seconds via Vercel Passport Over 2,000 projects created by hundreds of internal builders Mercor connects hundreds of thousands of domain experts with frontier AI labs, helping those labs generate the human data they need to train and evaluate leading models. It also runs large batches of automated grading jobs to evaluate models for labs and enterprises. Demand arrives in bursts that can push model traffic to peak capacity for days, even as individual evaluation or labeling jobs carry 24-hour deadlines. With so little time to deliver, requests waiting on a provider’s rate limits can put a client’s deadline at risk. Mercor’s business teams also need applications tailored to each engagement, giving experts a way to see their tasks and progress without waiting for changes to the core platform. For Aaron Brown, Mercor’s Head of Security, enabling more people to build means making it easier to give them the access they need and keep track of how they use it. Mercor uses Vercel AI Gateway to manage model access and Vercel Passport to handle secure access to their applications. When model capacity becomes a customer deadline Mercor’s mix of direct integrations and third-party gateways could not provide enough token-per-minute capacity for its open-model workloads when demand surged. As requests hit provider limits and entered retry queues, time-sensitive batch jobs stretched beyond 12 hours, consuming more than half of a client’s 24-hour deadline. AI Gateway provided more inference capacity and failover routing between providers when requests hit rate limits, helping batch work continue instead of waiting in retry queues. Mercor reports that those jobs now finish in 2 to 3 hours, leaving more time to complete the rest of the client’s work. In its first 10 days on Gateway, the team routed 18 million requests and 63 billion tokens, without hitting rate limits. Mercor continues to use multiple gateways and vendors, valuing Vercel for its combination of model access, controls, and hands-on support when the team needs more capacity. Engineers also get one API for leading foundation model providers and a growing catalog of open models, so they can try a new model without building another provider integration. Giving engineers room to experiment within limits As model use grew, Mercor needed to understand where token spend was going, but its previous setup offered little visibility into usage by team and project. title: F3 Lightning: How Meta Accelerates Ads ML Features to Production at Scale
excerpt: Facebook Feature Framework (F3) is Meta’s framework for authoring, compiling, and serving the machine learning features underlying ads ranking models, where a single request can require more than 20,000 features. We first presented F3 at AI @ Scale 2020 . F3 reduced execution computational costs by compiling all features into a single merged graph, but that graph also served as the release unit, so a single failure or invalid definition blocked the entire release pipeline. This post introduces F3 Lightning , an infrastructure layer built on top of F3 to resolve this challenge by decoupling feature releases from shared execution, so each feature is compiled, validated, deployed, and rolled back independently. The hardest part to solve was preserving F3’s efficiency improvements. Early per-feature release prototypes increased CPU usage because independent features no longer shared computation. We aimed to close this gap through four optimizations: stable computation identifiers, a single shared execution plan, one shared memory buffer across all features, and dense index mapping for direct array access. With F3 Lightning, comparable extraction features now reach production ~3.6x faster than the prior F3, with no increase in infrastructure compute cost. This shorter release cycle also enables more model iterations in the same period. A Primer on F3’s Shared Execution Architecture Production machine learning systems rarely consume raw data directly. Before a model can make a prediction, its feature-serving system may need to read stored signals, filter events to a time window, count or sum values, normalize them, and combine intermediate results. The simplest design to complete this work treats every feature as an independent function. That is easy to understand, but it becomes wasteful at scale, because features are not computationally independent. A seven-day click count and a seven-day impression count may read the same event source and apply the same time-window filter. A click-through rate feature may then reuse both results. Running each feature separately would repeat that filter, and every other shared step, on every request. F3 approached this differently, by representing feature extraction as a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Each node performs one unit of work, such as reading an input, applying a filter, or calculating an aggregation. An edge means one computation depends on the result of another. The graph’s outputs are the feature values a model consumes. Engineers author each feature independently in a high-level language. The F3 compiler turns each definition into a small graph, then merges the graphs for every feature a service uses into one merged graph (Figure 1). Where features share an operation, such as the seven-day filter above, the compiler collapses the duplicates into a single node. That shared work then runs once per request, not once for every feature that needs it. At runtime, feature extraction is a traversal of this merged graph. Figure 1: F3 consolidates all features into one merged graph. The Shared Graph Made Every Release All-or-Nothing F3’s merged graph shared computation efficiently, but it came with a major catch: The graph was also the release, and one malformed definition could hold back every other feature in the merged graph. Figure 2 illustrates this challenge. It shows seven independently authored features, A through G, where five definitions are valid, but D and G contain unrelated errors. The “Attempt 1” build fails on D, so none of the seven features ships. After D is corrected, the “Attempt 2” build reaches G and fails again. Only after both definitions are fixed in “Attempt 3” does the complete merged graph make it successfully to production. Figure 2: One failing feature blocks the entire release. Failures became more frequent as F3 scaled. F3 originally served a few hundred features, and at that size merges succeeded and releases were largely smooth. Today that number is more than
summary: Meta built F3 Lightning, a new layer for its ads machine learning system that lets each feature be released on its own instead of all together. Comparable features now reach production about 3.6 times faster, with no extra computing cost.

title: Introducing Zero Wire, a hub for investigating critical Internet vulnerabilities
excerpt: You run security at your organization. It’s 7:00 am, and you’re having breakfast. You receive a ping: a new critical vulnerability has been disclosed. Your team scrambles to compare vendor advisories, read technical research, check which systems run the affected software, and answer familiar questions from the business: are we affected, and what are we doing about it? Another disclosure arrives before that work is finished. AI is changing both the volume and speed of critical vulnerability discovery. It can analyze large codebases at scale and surface deeply nested flaws that may have existed for years without being found through human review. That discovery momentum will put more pressure on security teams to understand the impact of each disclosure on their infrastructure. To help security teams prepare, today we’re introducing Zero Wire : a public vulnerability intelligence feed on Cloudflare Radar, bringing the clarity of a news wire service to critical security developments. It helps security leaders and practitioners understand significant vulnerabilities and decide what to do next. How it works Zero Wire lives inside Cloudflare Radar under the security section. Each briefing brings together a plain-language explanation of the vulnerability, who should investigate it, recommended actions, and links to the evidence and vendor guidance. The format is deliberately simple: an index card with what you need to know, without the drama. A CISO should be able to understand the issue quickly and ask the right questions. An engineer should be able to follow the same briefing to the technical guidance needed to investigate and remediate it. We also offer a pre-compiled prompt you can use with your agent to assess the impact on your infrastructure. Cloudflare contributes security research, observations from our network, and practical knowledge of the controls that can help reduce exposure. The information is useful whether or not you are a Cloudflare customer. Zero Wire brings that context together with authoritative external sources, giving readers a starting point for assessment and a place to return as an issue develops. Our focus Rather than a catalog of every CVE, Zero Wire complements vendor advisories and vulnerability databases, linking readers to the evidence and technical guidance needed to act. Zero Wire focuses on critical CVEs in Internet-facing software, such as vulnerabilities in web applications, the runtimes and libraries they depend on, and services exposed to the Internet, where a proxy can help mitigate exploitation. We select significant issues that security teams need to understand and assess. Each briefing explains the potential impact, which deployments should be investigated, what is known about exploitation, and the available mitigation and patching guidance. A vulnerability’s severity and evidence of active exploitation are distinct: readers need both to make informed decisions. A dedicated Cloudflare protection, such as Web Application Firewall (WAF) rules, is not a prerequisite for inclusion. Some issues require vendor updates or changes beyond the traffic Cloudflare can inspect. Where Cloudflare controls can help, we explain their scope and configuration requirements. A walk through Zero Wire Start on the Zero Wire homepage . Each card introduces an issue, identifies associated CVEs where applicable, and summarizes why it matters and what to do. You can search for a published briefing using a CVE or issue name, and follow technology tags to related entries. One briefing can cover several related CVEs when understanding them together makes the response clearer. Find what needs attention The homepage separates briefings into two categories. “Needs attention” brings together issues requiring active assessment or action, including those with known exploitation or developing guidance. “Reference” keeps briefings available when guidance has stabilized. Moving to “Reference” does not mean every affected system
summary: Cloudflare has launched Zero Wire, a public feed on its Radar site that explains serious internet security flaws in plain language. Each short briefing says who should look into an issue, what to do next, and links to the evidence and vendor guidance.

title: How we halved DNS build delay and cut memory use by 85%
excerpt: When I last wrote about our DNS propagation pipeline in 2022 , the Zone Builder received about 250 DNS record changes per second. Today it receives about 700, nearly three times as many, plus about 100 other events, such as zone setting changes. However, the number of events was never the real problem. The problem was the kind of work some of those events needed, and how that work grows with the size of a zone. Some zones now hold more than 20 million records, and we expect them to keep growing toward hundreds of millions. Each event starts a clock that measures how long it takes us to turn that change into data our authoritative DNS servers can use. We call that work a build. A build reads the current database state, converts it into the format used at the edge, and writes any changes to Quicksilver . In 2022, per-record builds were 150 times faster than full builds on average. On a test zone with one million records, per-record builds were 4,250 times faster. We ended that post with the obvious next step: do the same thing for zone settings. Why doesn't the Zone Builder just rebuild the setting that changed? It should, and that is where we ended up. However, proving when it was safe took most of the work. A record event identifies what changed. A zone event can come from many Cloudflare products, may not say why the zone changed, and can alter data shared by several zones with the same name. Choosing too much work wastes capacity. Choosing too little can leave stale or incorrect DNS data at the edge. We built a targeted build planner that chooses the smallest build we can prove is safe, and a new scheduler that combines work for the same zone. Zone setting changes no longer rebuild zones with tens of millions of records. Together, they cut peak memory by 85%, and the extra headroom let us safely shorten waits the pipeline has always needed for resilience, halving the time from a DNS change to its data being written to Quicksilver. How DNS changes reach the edge A DNS zone is the collection of records and settings for a domain. Cloudflare uses a multi-stage pipeline to turn a change to that zone into data available across our global network . A customer changes a DNS record through the DNS Records API or dashboard, or another Cloudflare service changes a zone setting. The change is stored in a database. The database change or another system produces a Kafka event. The DNS Kafka Aggregator combines events from several Kafka topics and sends them to the Zone Builder. The Zone Builder reads the required zone data and converts it into keys understood by our authoritative DNS servers. The Zone Builder compares those keys with Quicksilver , our distributed key-value store. It writes only what changed, and Quicksilver propagates those changes across Cloudflare's network. This is a simplified view. The Zone Builder does not copy database rows directly to the edge. It combines records with zone settings, applies DNS serving rules, and organizes the result so our authoritative DNS servers can read it quickly. Why full builds stopped scaling The original Zone Builder had one useful property: it did not need to know why a zone changed. It rebuilt the desired state from the current database state. Read the current zone and its settings. Read every DNS record in the zone. Convert those records into Quicksilver keys. Compare the new keys with those already stored. Remove stale keys, write changed keys, and update zone metadata. The final write contains only changed keys. However, a full build still reads, encodes, and compares every record, and holds the whole zone in memory while it does so. That is cheap for a small zone. For our largest zones, with tens of millions of records, the zone does not fit in memory at all. I explain how we handle that below. Zone settings made targeting harder. Universal SSL is one example. Enabling or disabling it updates metadata and can change Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) records at the zone a
summary: Cloudflare changed how it updates DNS data for its largest zones. Zone setting changes now rebuild only what they need, cutting peak memory by 85% and halving the time for a DNS change to reach the edge.

title: AWS Weekly Roundup: GPT-6.1 Terra on Bedrock, Step Functions as agent tools, and more (November 2, 2026)
excerpt: The agentic launches that stayed with me last week had nothing to do with how capable a model is. They were about reach. AWS Step Functions , which already orchestrates over 220 AWS services, can now be handed to an agent as a tool, so workflows teams already trust became callable without a rewrite. In the same week, the AI blog published how one engagement platform exposed roughly 400 internal API operations the same way. Neither story involves rebuilding anything, only describing what exists and letting the agent find it. The other thread was cost. OpenAI’s newest Terra model reached Amazon Bedrock priced well below the model beside it, and two post-quantum launches landed for a deadline nobody can put on a calendar yet. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news… Headlines OpenAI GPT-6.1 Terra is now generally available on Amazon Bedrock , and what interests me is where it sits rather than what it tops. Terra is the everyday-workload line of the GPT-6 family. In OpenAI’s Agents’ Last Exam evaluation it scored 15 percentage points higher than GPT-5.6 Terra, performed on par with GPT-6 Astra, and completed tasks more than three times faster than both. Those are OpenAI’s figures, not an independent test. The price is what I would check first: input and output tokens are at least 50% lower than GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-5.6 Terra. It takes up to 1 million input tokens with text and image input, and you can reach it from the Bedrock APIs or ChatGPT Work and Codex. AWS Step Functions workflows are now available as AI agent tools through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, which connects agents to tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The division of labor is the idea: the agent decides when to run a workflow and what input to pass; Step Functions runs each step exactly as you defined it. A support agent can trigger a refund, and the eligibility check, the manager approval, and the credit still happen in that order every time, because the ordering was never the model’s to improvise. Your existing Standard and Express workflows qualify as connector targets, and agents can also look up runs. It’s available in all Regions where AgentCore Gateway is, at standard rates. Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention: AWS Key Management Service now supports ML-KEM for post-quantum key encapsulation – You can now establish a shared secret with a post-quantum algorithm using AWS KMS keys, with private keys in FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated HSMs. All three NIST FIPS 203 parameter sets are supported through Encapsulate , which produces a random 32-byte shared secret and its ciphertext, and Decapsulate , which recovers it. The threat is harvest now, decrypt later: an adversary records today’s key exchange and recovers the secret once quantum computers are powerful enough. It’s available everywhere KMS runs except the Middle East (UAE and Bahrain) and China Regions. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL added post-quantum TLS key exchange the same week, on versions 18 and higher. AWS IAM Identity Center now supports cross-Region trusted identity propagation – You can now carry a user’s identity with their request to AWS services in another Region. This removes a genuine architectural constraint: trusted identity propagation used to require every service accessing that identity to sit in the same Region, which left two unappealing options, broad IAM roles that cannot distinguish individual users, or consolidating all your services into a single Region. Now the identity travels with the request automatically, so you grant access by user and group membership and audit who accessed what. It’s available at no additional cost everywhere IAM Identity Center runs. Amazon ECS now supports GPU sharing with NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS) – You can now run multiple Amazon ECS tasks concurrently on a single NVIDIA GPU, the practical answer to work that only ever uses a fraction of one, like small-model inference and
summary: AWS lets AI agents trigger its existing Step Functions workflows as tools, so steps like approvals run in a fixed order. OpenAI's Terra model is now on Amazon Bedrock at least 50% cheaper than comparable models, per OpenAI's own figures.
